transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm explaining this right, and I really don't want to waste your time if it's just... normal stress, you know? 

But I guess I'm here because I keep getting these, um, these awful doubts that I've missed something important. I'm a graphic designer, so I've always been detail-oriented, but lately... I don't know, I'll start worrying that I got a number wrong on the mortgage payment, or missed a tiny clause in a client proof, or even just left a door not latched. 

And the silly thing is, even when I absolutely know I checked it—and I really am usually very put-together, I promise—the thought just barges back in anyway. It's like my brain just says, 'What if this is the mistake that costs you everything?' 

I'm sorry, I know that sounds a bit dramatic. Does that make sense? Is that the kind of thing you help people with?

When these doubts come up, do you find yourself doing specific things—like checking repeatedly, counting, or trying to neutralize the thought in some way—to feel more certain or to prevent something bad from happening?

Um, well... yes, a little bit, I suppose. I mean, I think it's normal to want to be thorough, right? So I do go back and check things. I'll just, um, reopen the design files a few times, or reread my client emails before I send them. And with the online payment confirmations, I'll log back in just to double-check. It's really just me trying to be careful, I promise. 

But... well, this is the part that's a little embarrassing to admit. I hope you don't think I'm completely neurotic, but sometimes I also catch myself repeating the numbers or the figures silently in my head. Just saying them over and over until they finally feel... I don't know, 'settled'? 

I try so hard to just push past it, but sometimes a simple invoice or a tiny logo revision ends up taking hours that I can't even bill the client for. Which I know isn't very professional or efficient of me, and I feel terrible about it. Does that... does that answer your question? I hope I'm giving you the right information.

Do these thoughts and behaviors ever interfere with your ability to get things done on time, or cause you a lot of stress that spills over into other parts of your life, like your relationships or your sleep?

Oh, um... well, I really try my best not to let it affect anyone else. I think everyone gets a little stressed about work sometimes, right? But... I guess, if I'm being completely honest—and I really hate to admit this, because I've always prided myself on being very reliable—it has been... well, it's been slowing me down. 

Like, work that used to just take me a quick afternoon is suddenly... it drags on for days. And because of that, I've had to push back a few deadlines. I've missed out on billable hours, too, because I obviously can't charge them for the extra time I spend just checking and re-checking my own files. 

And, um... this is really hard to say, but one of my longtime clients actually reached out recently. They asked me if I could still handle their simple revisions on time. It was just... it was mortifying, honestly. I feel so terrible about it. I promise I'm trying really hard to get back on track so I don't let anyone else down. 

Does that... is that the kind of thing you meant? I hope I'm not sounding completely incompetent.
How much time do these checking behaviors and mental rituals usually take each day, on average?

Um, well... I haven't really timed it, exactly. I mean, I don't want to make it sound worse than it is, because I really do try to just get on with my day. 

I suppose if you added it all up, it might be... maybe a couple of hours? Or, well, maybe a little more on a bad day when I have a lot of client files due. But it's not like I'm just sitting there doing it all at once! It's just a few minutes here, a few minutes there, you know? Just trying to be careful. 

I'm sure lots of people spend time double-checking their work, right? I really hope it doesn't sound like I'm just wasting my whole day. Is... is a couple of hours normal for this sort of thing?

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including intrusive doubts, repetitive checking behaviors, mental rituals, and significant impairment in functioning, strongly align with OCD (F42.9). Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) is less likely due to the presence of specific obsessive-compulsive features rather than free-floating anxiety. Major depressive disorder (F32.9) is not currently supported by the history, as there is no report of depressed mood, anhedonia, or other depressive symptoms.
